genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs the kitchen of a country inn
she started out on a very cramped cooking station
at first she followed written instructions to the letter
she weighed every ingredient and was afraid of getting things wrong
she now trusts her palate rather than a timer
she has given up fierce heat and prefers a very gentle simmer
her old way of cooking leaned on an abundance of spices
her current way of cooking leans on the worth of the raw ingredient
she passes this change on to the beginners she trains regularly
she holds that mastering the hands comes before mastering the wait
text: The woman who runs the kitchen at a country inn learned her trade on a cooking station barely wider than her shoulders. Back then she read recipes line by line, weighed out every ingredient, and lived in fear of getting something wrong. These days she tastes, adjusts, and lets a pot sit without once glancing at a timer, since her own tongue tells her sooner than any clock would. Heat used to be her tool for speed; now she wants the barest tremble on the surface, because a slow simmer draws out flavor that a hard boil tears apart. Her old cooking leaned on a heavy hand with spices. Her cooking now leans on what the ingredient itself is worth. She hands that shift to the beginners who come through her kitchen each season, telling them the same thing every time: waiting is harder to learn than the work of the hands.

units: the place described sits beside a waterway
the staff put down the dishes quietly and without explanation
the list of dishes is short and fits on a single sheet
that list shifts with what comes in
the shortness of the offering suggests nothing is kept in store for long
the cooking methods are of uneven quality
the fish is right on the surface and right inside
the root vegetables are spoiled by a sauce that weighs too much
the last sweet dish rescues the impression left by the vegetables
the closing verdict urges a visit despite too much sauce
text: Three things stand out in this dining room set beside a canal. Start with the service, spare to the point of silence: plates come down quietly, set in front of you without a word, and nobody offers to tell you what is on them. Then the menu, a single sheet that shifts with whatever comes in from the growers, listing so few dishes that clearly nothing sits waiting in a cold room. Last, the cooking, which is where the kitchen wobbles. Fish comes off the pan with crisp skin and flesh that holds together, while the roots beneath it drown in a thick sauce that blurs every edge. Dessert wins the argument back and rights what the roots had spoiled: a smooth cream, barely sweet, with fruit poached in its own juice. Worth the trip, then, as long as you accept that sauce here sometimes takes up more room than it ought to.

units: the writer of the message tells about a cooking attempt from the evening before
he browned sliced bulbs in a wide flat pan
he stirred without stopping so the fat would not turn black
he then added pulses and water
the pot cooked slowly while he cleaned up
the first taste had no flavor at all
he set the seasoning right with a sour fruit and crushed seeds
he covered the dish with a tart milk product
someone from the same building took three helpings
the writer admits he made the dish up with no model to follow
text: You will never guess what came out of my tiny kitchen last night. Onions went into a wide pan first, sliced thin, and I stood over them the whole time, stirring, because the fat was one moment away from turning black. In went the lentils, then cold water, and the pot ticked along on a low flame while I dealt with the washing up. A taste later: nothing. Flat as paper. So I squeezed in citrus juice, crushed a pinch of seeds over the top, and the whole thing woke up at once. I poured off the extra liquid, spooned soured milk across the surface, and carried it to the table with no faith in it at all. A neighbor from two doors along, asked over at the last minute, went back for a third helping and wanted to know how it was made. I owned up: there was no recipe behind any of it, and I had made the whole thing up as I went.

units: the text explains where the golden shade of a bread crust comes from
the color arises from a meeting between sugars and matter bearing nitrogen
very dry air sets that meeting going
a pale surface points to an oven that is not hot enough
too much water in the dough holds the color back as well
damp keeps the surface from reaching the temperature it needs
heat pushed too far turns the sugars black
that drift brings a bitter taste
a very dark crust is not necessarily a fault
one and the same change yields pleasant scents and burnt ones
text: What turns a crust amber? Apprentice bakers ask it constantly, and the answer lies in a meeting between the sugars of the dough and the proteins alongside them, a meeting that only the dry heat of the baking chamber can set going. And when the surface stays pale? Usually the air lacks bite, or the dough carries too much water: steam holds the color back, since damp keeps the surface from climbing past the point where the change begins. Push the heat harder, and what happens? The sugars caramelize, then blacken, and a bitter edge settles over everything. Does a very dark crust mean, then, that somebody got it wrong? Not at all. The shade you aim for depends on the smell you want, because one and the same change gives you the scent of toasted nuts and the scent of scorching alike.

units: a spice seller sees his shop falling quiet
visitors smell the goods but walk out with nothing
their holding back comes from not knowing what to do with these products
his student reckons a scent on its own does not bring a sale
she suggests keeping a tasting pot on the counter
plants would steep in it in a seasoned liquid
the seller worries at first about the lack of room
he ends up taking up the idea
sales climb from the following week on
visitors come back with sharper requests
text: On a wet evening the spice seller was complaining that his shop was going quiet for want of curious customers. He told his apprentice how people wandered in, leaned over the jars, breathed deep, and then walked out with nothing, put off by powders they had no idea what to do with. She answered that a smell convinces nobody until it belongs to a dish. Her idea was plain enough: keep a pot at one end of the counter with roots steeping in a seasoned broth, so anyone could taste before buying. He balked, sure it would swallow the little space he had, and then gave way. By the second week he admitted the jars were emptying and that the same faces kept coming back with sharper questions. His shop, he said with dry amusement, had stopped selling powder and started selling suppers.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text sets two great ways of keeping food against each other, both older than machine-made cold
the first way takes the water out of the food
salt, sugar and a spell in dry air belong to that way
denying the tiny living things their water stops them from spreading
the second way changes the matter through souring or fermenting
the ferments themselves build a setting that germs cannot bear
taking the water out stiffens the texture and forces a soak before use
changing the matter plainly alters the taste of the food
it raises scents the raw matter never held
cold halts spoiling without adding anything to the flavor
text: Long before anyone could make cold on demand, two families of technique competed for the work of keeping food, and the contest still lights up the kitchens of today. The first works by taking away: salt, sugar or a spell in dry air pull water out of the tissue, and the small living things that spoil food lose the medium they cannot do without. The second works by changing: matter steeps in a sour brine, or ferments are left to build a setting no intruder survives. Taking away leaves the first taste mostly alone, yet it hardens the flesh and forces a soak before anything can be done with it. Changing rewrites the flavor outright, souring, rounding, raising scents the raw thing never held. Cold came last, and it halts decay while creating nothing, which explains both its reign and its blandness.

units: the text lays out four ways of carrying heat in cooking
boiling water spreads a steady heat that goes no higher
it softens the tough parts and draws out the aromas that dissolve
cooking with steam avoids washing the substance out of the food
it holds the color and the firmness of vegetables
heated fat climbs above the temperature water can reach
it serves to brown the surface before the flame comes down
the dry heat of a closed chamber dries the outside and concentrates the sugars
the piece has to be moistened with its own cooking juices
chaining these ways in a thought-out order gives results no single one can reach
text: Four ways of moving heat cover nearly everything done in a home kitchen, and each obeys a logic of its own. Boiling water gives an even, moderate heat: it softens tough tissue, pulls out whatever aromas dissolve, and suits any dish meant to yield a broth. Steam is gentler and cooks without washing the substance out of the food, which is how greens keep both their color and their bite. Hot fat climbs well above the temperature water can reach and builds a browned surface, which is why cooks sear in it before dropping the flame. The dry air of a closed oven, last of the four, parches the outside and concentrates the sugars, provided the piece gets basted with its own juices along the way. String the four together in a thought-out order and you get textures that no single one of them will ever hand you.

units: a large wedding feast is put at risk by a cooking mishap
the woman in charge of the sauces left her pan on a source of heat
she had stepped away to see to a helper who had hurt his hand
the bottom of the pan had taken on a blackened deposit
the guests were already waiting to be served
she brought the deposit back by pouring pale wine over it
the deposit gave off a smell of nuts
she strained the liquid and enriched it with cold fat
a relative of the bride asked how it had been done
she would not set the method down in writing
text: A wedding feast came close to collapse over one forgotten pan. The cook in charge of the sauces had left her reduction sitting on a hot plate while she saw to an apprentice who had opened his finger on a blade. She came back to a dark, sticky crust welded to the bottom, and the hall out front was already waiting. Rather than start over, she poured in a glass of pale wine, scraped hard with a spatula, and found that the burnt layer was giving off a warm smell of nuts nobody expected. Through a sieve it went, a knob of cold butter beaten in, and the sauce reached the tables with nobody the wiser. The bride's father was asking for the recipe before dessert. She told the story to the other cooks at length, but write the method down she would not: an accident, she said, cannot be ordered up.

units: the instructions cover the roasting of a whole farmyard bird
it has to come out of the cold well before it is cooked
without that wait the outside would be done before the middle
the skin has to be wiped, because water blocks the browning
as long as water is leaving it, the surface does not get hot enough
the bird has to sit on a support with gaps in it
left flat in its own juices, the underside would cook in water
the piece has to be moistened with its fat while it roasts
a rest after roasting is needed before carving
carving too soon loses the juices and leaves the meat dry
text: Take a whole farmyard bird and set it out of the cold a good long while before it goes anywhere near heat, or the outside will be done long before the middle even warms. Wipe the skin dry with a cloth: damp skin will not brown, because the surface cannot climb past the temperature browning needs while water is still leaving it. Salt it well and stand it on a rack, never flat in its own juices, or the underside boils instead of roasting. Spoon the fat that melts out of it back over the skin as it roasts, since hot liquid carries heat into the hollows that air reaches badly. Then let it rest away from the flame before you carve, because tightened fibers give their juice back as they cool. Cut into it too soon and the whole of it runs out onto the board, and what you serve is dry.

units: amounts of damaged vegetables were thrown out when the market closed
the sellers were sorry about the loss and could do nothing about it
the goods were still fit to eat despite the way they looked
no arrangement existed to take them away before closing time
a group of people living nearby put forward an answer in three steps
the unsold stock is gathered in the closing hour
a room lent by the town is used for sorting
the vegetables are cooked and put into jars that same evening
the food is handed to households named by the welfare service
the shortage of room and the want of cold storage hold the scheme back
text: Whole crates of bruised vegetables went into the dumpster every week when the covered market shut, under the eyes of the stallholders themselves, sorry about it and out of ideas. The produce was sound, only dented or a shade too ripe to sell, and nothing existed to carry it off before nightfall. A residents' group put forward an answer in three moves: gather the unsold stock in the closing hour, sort it in a room lent by the town, and turn it into soup and preserves right away. Volunteers simmer the vegetables that same evening, sterilize the jars, and pass them on to families sent their way by the welfare service. The traders say their bills for waste collection have come down. What holds the scheme back now is room: the lent space is full, and a cold store is still missing.
